message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
The proposal is to raise the weekend room rate from £145 to £165 and add a two-night minimum for Saturday stays. It projects at least £204,000 a year in extra revenue.

The rate rise is probably justified, because Harbourside is priced well below competitors. But the evidence offered for it doesn't show what the proposal says. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count. And the two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's largest Saturday customer group.

## 1. The June-to-July rise in occupancy is seasonal, not a response to price

The proposal's key evidence is that weekend occupancy went from 81% in June to 89% in July after the £10 rise. But the proposal's own Table 1 and text explain July differently: it is the start of the hotel's peak season, with the harbour festival and school holidays. August reached 93%. Occupancy would have risen in July whatever the rate.

Two further problems:
- **Timing:** the rate rose in the last week of June. Many July stays would already have been booked at the old rate, so July occupancy partly reflects bookings made before the increase.
- **The right comparison:** look at July–December 2025 against the same months in 2024, at the old rates. If occupancy held up, that is real evidence the guests aren't price-sensitive.

The value-for-money score of 8.4 is good news. But it was measured at the lower prices, so it doesn't predict how guests will react at £165.

## 2. The revenue figure uses 124 rooms; the hotel has 112

Section 2 gives **112 rooms**, but Section 5 calculates with **124**. At 112 rooms, the same method gives about **£184,000**, not £204,000.

That figure is still too high, because it applies the £20 rise to every occupied weekend room. The proposal itself says the rise won't apply to all of them:
- **Wedding blocks** make up about 38% of Saturday-night bookings. They are booked through the couple, so they are group rates, not the standard rate.
- **Corporate and group contracted rates** are honoured at their existing prices.
- **Online travel agents** take a commission on the bookings they make, so the hotel doesn't keep the whole £20 on those.

Only the rooms sold at the standard rate gain £20. Depending on that share, a realistic figure could be well under £150,000. The proposal should calculate it from the actual mix of booking types.

## 3. The two-night minimum clashes with wedding business

Wedding guests make up 38% of Saturday-night bookings. They "arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning," which is exactly the single-night stay the minimum would rule out. Only *already contracted* groups are protected, so future wedding blocks would fall under the rule. The likely outcomes are:
- couples sending guests to other hotels;
- Quayside Hall recommending other hotels;
- a weaker relationship with the venue next door.

More generally, the minimum only helps on Saturdays that would sell out anyway. That happened on 31 Saturdays in 2025. On the other Saturdays, a one-night guest who doesn't want two nights may simply book elsewhere.

The unquantified two-night effect could therefore be negative. So "£204,000 is a floor" doesn't hold.

A narrower rule would capture the benefit with less risk: apply the minimum only on high-demand dates, and exempt wedding and other group blocks.

## 4. The rate rise has a useful safety margin

The current rate of £145 at 79% occupancy gives the same room revenue as £165 at about **69%** occupancy. So occupancy at standard-rate prices could fall by about 10 points before room revenue drops. That margin is narrower once spending on food and drink is included, since fewer guests also means less of that.

This matters for the monitoring plan. Triggering a review at a 5-point fall is sensible, well before revenue is lost. Tracking bookings weekly against the same weeks in 2025 is also the right method.

A monthly occupancy figure, though, only shows what was booked weeks earlier. Weekly booking pace is the early warning, and it is worth saying so explicitly.

## What holds

- **The competitor gap is real.** At £165, Harbourside would match the cheapest hotel in its competitive set.
- **The arithmetic is internally consistent:** the 2025 average weekend occupancy of 79%, and £204,000 on the 124-room figure.
- **Protecting corporate and contracted group rates** is right, as is giving online travel agents two weeks' notice.
- **The monitoring plan** compares like-for-like weeks and sets a trigger below the break-even point.

## On the author's description

- **"A direct test" of price sensitivity.** The June-to-July rise is seasonal, and many July stays were booked at the old rate.
- **"£204,000 is a floor."** The figure uses 124 rooms instead of 112 and applies the rise to rooms that won't pay it. The two-night minimum could reduce revenue.
- **"Corporate and group commitments are protected."** Only contracted ones are, and future wedding blocks are not.
- **The competitor gap, the value-for-money score and the monitoring plan** are as described.

## Recommendation

- **Approve the rate rise.** The competitor gap and the break-even margin support it.
- **Re-cost it on 112 rooms,** counting only rooms sold at the standard rate.
- **Replace the June–July evidence** with a year-on-year comparison.
- **Narrow the two-night minimum** to high-demand dates and exempt wedding and other group blocks, or trial it on a few weekends first.
